utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, witness, again. Do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I'd like us to come back incident number four, number six, we are talking about the same thing. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Instead of nodding, you could you give a loud answer because to translate nodding is very difficult.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, this depends on the experience of the doctor who is carrying out the examination, that is the first fact. So the doctor has to make a diagnosis of the injuries so it's not for him -- it's not a primary task to see what's the exit, what's the entry, just that the injury that he has to treat. If there are two injuries, he then has to see whether they are linked by a channel so that what would be injured on that trajectory from the entry to the exit point and possibly someone who has experience, more or less a doctor, would be able to see the size and the form of the wound but that would depend on the treating doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. What interests me is the document that we had a look at together and that was the report in relation to the incident about the injury. Do you know which document I'm talking about?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the document that we read yesterday, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Indeed. Professor, how many days did it pass between the moment of the injury, when the injury occurred, and when this document was written?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a report from the hospital and that was compiled on the day of admission, on the 25th of June, 1993, 25th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, and here, right at the bottom, this report is done immediately but then I can see that there is a date, 11th of the 11th, 1995, I don't know what that is, I don't know when that was issued. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. If this report is compiled immediately, and if it is compared to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President this is beyond the scope of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to express myself but of course the presence of the witness is an obstacle to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would just indicate where in cross-examination the matter has been dealt with to start with, I think that would not influence the witness as something he has been present.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, very well, but the problem is between the date, but I don't know whether Mr. Mundis wishes to speak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to address the Chamber in the absence of the witness, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then if -- now both parties are asking the witness to leave the courtroom. Professor Dunjic, I have to ask you to leave, accompanied by the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis, I think it would be -- you would like to do it in private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: It doesn't need to be, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But perhaps since Mr. Piletta-Zanin first asked to explain how it derives from the cross-examination I would first like to give him the opportunity and then hear from you, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. The question that I wanted to ask that would be the last question to the witness and this is just chronologically speaking in terms of factual experience. We know that as time goes by we forget things and things can happen, the position of things we can forget. Therefore, if this certificate, this document was written immediately after or very quickly after the fact occurred I think that the people who issued it at the time they had a much clearer vision of what the injury was at the time including the difference between the entry and exit wounds. And of course if a person is injured, they don't know exactly how they were injured, perhaps in the back, but then what happens is that the witness will maybe forget. So my problem is a chronological problem, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand your problem, but is this in the expertise of this expert witness, that's my problem, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. I don't know, as far as the witness just testified, that the report was made on the 25th of June, 1993, whether that is true or not, I don't know. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I just add something, Mr. President? I don't know to what extent a scar can heal in the course of time, that is, I don't know how we can see through a scar where was the entry, where was the exit wound. It can happen that the injury before it closes, we can then see where the exit and the entry wounds are. I don't know whether it is the same situation after the scar appears, after the wound is healed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes so the first question would be were the scars of entry or exit wounds are disappearing and if they do not disappear they are still there, that's -- Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could draw to your attention the second -- page of the English translation of the medical report it indicates that the date of 11 November 1995 is handwritten along with three signatures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would also draw to the Trial Chamber's attention the fact that on 11 November 1995 the victim to which this medical report refers was interviewed by investigators from the Office of the Prosecutor and made a statement which was signed on the 11th of November, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I don't have copies of that statement available in the courtroom, Mr. President, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But let me just ask you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, is part of your position that this document was created on the 11th of November or -- no, so therefore there seems to be no confusion about that. Then Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you can ask the questions but let's keep in mind not to tell stories to the witness and ask his comment but to ask him a question and the first one would then be whether the scars would disappear.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, as usual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you please escort Professor Dunjic into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, my question is as follows: If, with the passage of time, do you know whether the scars, whether they are the scars of the entry wound or the exit wound, do you know whether the scars disappear with the passage of time?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If these wounds are in question, the scars remain permanently. The scar just changes its colour, its first pink and then it becomes pale and it's on the basis of the colour of the scar that we can determine how old the wound is. And the scar, in general, has an irregular form which is supposed to close off the point of contact of the projectile with the skin, because this is where the defect is inflicted on the skin. This scar can be fairly regular, it can also be sort of under the skin, it depends on the reaction of the tissue itself and also depends on medical intervention, will whether medical intervention was performed on the wound itself in order to clean the wound et cetera. So this scar always remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Doctor, Professor, I apologise. If, for example, a professional such as yourself examined the wounded party of the body of the victim we are talking about, would it be possible for such a person to determine the point of entry and the exit point?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Judge Nieto-Navia has questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Yesterday you were talking about the medical documents and you said in some of the incidents you had at hand a medical documents, in other incidents you didn't have the documents and you said the following: "I have to say there was such cases where the witness was not at all hurt." I take it that most of the witnesses were not hurt at all, but my question is were you referring to witnesses or the victims? Do you want me to quote you again? You said, "I have to say, there was such cases where the witness," and I noted that, "was not actual hurt." My question is were you referring to witnesses or to victims?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that was correctly translated. I said that in certain cases, individual cases, I didn't have medical documentation but in some cases, the victims hadn't been examined, the wounded hadn't been examined. Witnesses had been examined. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: That is different.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: You were asked about the position of the bodies; do you remember that, on a given incident and you said the following: "If we don't know this position, then we are unable to determine the position from which, let's say, the projectile came". Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: My question is the following: Normally, I would say the victim is removed from the place in which he is wounded, even in cases in which you don't know whether the victim is already dead or not, the body is removed. So my question is: How do you know which was the position the victim at that very moment?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me to elaborate on this. That's the essence of everything that I have tried to present to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you are suffering from technical problems?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For the interpreters, the problem is the microphone, as far as I understand. Yes, yes -- no -- the interpreters asked you to use the microphone but I was explaining that you might not be able to do so. A new microphone for Mr. Piletta-Zanin, please. I take it that we can continue and see whether the problem could be solved. Yes. Yes, Professor Dunjic, you just started to give an explanation and --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll be brief. When we said that we determined the position of the body of an injured party, our first and main parameter is the wound channel, the entry wound and the exit wound, the location of the entry wound and the exit wound. Let's say that this is a certain individual, if you'll view this from above, the entry could be the right part of the rib cage and the projectile goes in this direction. It comes out at the back and its direction goes upwards. Yesterday, I said that we determined the nature of the wound on the basis of the physiological position of the body when performing an autopsy and when we examine a human body regardless of whether the person is dead or not. We have a look at the channel, it goes from the right to the left, from bottom upwards but what is important here if we have a look at the body from the side, if we look at the body in profile, it can go upwards, the channel can go upwards so we have three dimensions of this channel in order to determine it. That's what the channel would look like, that's what would be the physiological position. Having determined the physiological position of the body it's important to hear what the injured party or other witnesses have to say. And if the witness or the injured party says that I was bent forwards or backwards when hit, that statement then has a certain weight in relation to the medical evidence and we compare such statements with the position is a person X or Y. That's where the person was hit in a position which the person mentioned or did not mention, we then determine the location from which that projectile may have come. We then have the point from which fire may have been opened and if that corresponds to the wound channel, then we say that that is the position of the injured party, as the injured party stated or as the witnesses stated. If we don't know the position from which fire was opened, we need to have two factors. We need to have the position of the body, that is the first thing, we have to know whether the person was crouching, was bent over, we need to know when the projectile arrived, and we need a medical document saying how the wound was described, in medical terms. So we need the position in order to draw a line, you have to know the channel of the wound here and the direction the projectile came from. From this position, or from this position towards the wound channel, and on the basis of the position of the body, we determine the direction from which the projectile came. We have to have two points which we have to link: The injured party and the position from which fire was opened if I've been sufficiently clear. So the channel, the channel within the body gives us the reason of saying the person was hit from the front and that was if someone had fired at me from down below, in this direction, but I wasn't in that position and then witnesses might say that I was in some other position. I still maintain the wound channel but in that case, the direction of the projectile is changed, the position from which that projectile came and hit me. So on the basis of witness statements and medical documents we try to determine the direction from which the projectile came in these particular situations in which I have described. Apart from certain witness statements and some medical documentation, I didn't have the necessary parameters in order to relate these two points to each other, the medical documents and the witness statements. I didn't have the material to establish a straight line between these two points in order to determine the direction from which the projectile came. That is how we determine the position of the body at the time that the person was wounded. We have to know the position from which fire was opened and we need to have medical facts that have been determined. If we don't know where fire was opened from then we use medical documents and witness statements and we relate the two points to each other and on that basis, establish the position from which fire was opened. What I said yesterday, on the basis of the look of the entry and exit wound, we determine the wound channel and everything that is specific to it; the type of projectile used that caused the entry wound and we determine whether that projectile came directly or not because the wound channel in the body can rebound from the first obstacle. For example, if it hit the skull, if it entered the skull let's say this is the skull, the channel could be here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: I'm sorry I have to interrupt you. If I understand you well, you're saying that physician can determine the entry and exit wounds and the channel through which the bullet pass.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: That's clear. But if you don't know the origin of fire, can you determine that origin taking into account the channel only?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second parameter which is missing. I have to determine the wound channel, the point of entry and the location of the entry wound and the location of the exit wound as an expert this is what I have to do. In order to determine the position from which fire is opened, the direction from which the projectile came, I need to have another piece of evidence, either the statement of a witness or of the injured party or the position where the person was hit. For example, if someone is hit in the head and the projectile enters at this point and comes out at this point and if the person is in an open space, in a field, the projectile didn't fall from the sky. I have to put him in a realistic position in which he could have been hit so that he could have been hit in the head if he had been bent, for example. So I can't say whether fire was opened from this direction or this direction, it depends on the direction he was facing but it's a fact that the projectile hit him here. If I have a witness who says yes, he was in this position, he was bent over, he was doing something, then on the basis of that witness statement which I can relate to the wound, on that basis I can come to the conclusion that the projectile came from a certain direction but from the position where the person was wound and -- the position where the person was wounded and the position from which the firearm opened fire, this is the work of the ballistics expert he has to determine this. So it is on this basis that we try to define the position of the body of a certain injured party. We have to compare the medical documents to the witness statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: So we need always a third information, the origin of the fire can be determined by the ballistic expert but only taking into account the position of the victim, if this position is known. If the position is not known then it is very difficult to determine the origin of fire unless you have another information.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ballistics expert has to determine that but only after one has determined the channel wound. If someone is sitting in this courtroom, for example, as I am and a projectile hits him from the back, that has to be determined, someone fired from the back, not from here. Whether I was sitting or standing is not relevant. That would be relevant if there was another wound in front of me and if there is a wound behind me, at the back as well. There have to be medical facts on the basis of which you can try to assess the statement given by the injured party and assess the witness statements, but if no one is present and I am wounded, then these -- then the material traces will determine my position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: We were checking on the transcript yesterday, the sentence that I quoted to you at the very beginning and it is exactly what I said, "I have to say, there was such cases where the witness was not at all hurt." It's page 19641, line 8. It's probably a problem of translation. Thank you, Professor, don't worry about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm familiar with that case. I apologise, but a witness was questioned who wasn't injured but the injured party wasn't questioned. That's incident number 22. The witness testified about a friend who had been injured, but the injured party wasn't questioned. Perhaps that's where the problem lies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor, no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge El Mahdi has one or more question for you as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. [Interpretation] Professor, I'd like you to inform me about one or two questions, given your expertise, a problem of a general nature. On the basis of your practical and academic knowledge in the course of an armed conflict, is it a rule to examine each incident as if the incident had occurred in normal circumstances but not in circumstances of war? On the basis of your professional expertise, when there is an armed conflict, are these medical examinations usually carried out for each incident, are the victims questioned, are the witnesses questioned, are the channels analysed, is the position of a given victim well-established?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I've understood you correctly, I'll answer your question from the medical point of view. In all cases, if someone has been fatally wounded, if someone was killed by a firearm and in extraordinary circumstances and in peacetime circumstances, autopsies are performed. Forensic medical autopsies, they are carried out in the standard manner. The procedure is well-known and such autopsies determine all the relevant facts that I have been talking about. If it appears to be necessary for there to be some sort of an expert report, then we have a valid document on the basis of which we can compile an expert report, the facts are established, and a record is made and the doctor who is treating a wounded person, he doesn't have to compile an expert report but he has to describe, with precision, what he established, what he did, what procedure he followed. That's the standard procedure and it doesn't matter whether the circumstances are extraordinary, the wounded person doesn't have to be treated immediately, he can be treated somewhere else, he is taken from the site and this is the case for witnesses too. Six months later or a year later the witness can give a statement, that doesn't matter but as an expert when compiling an expert report I'll take this into consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. If I've understood you correctly you say when there is ongoing conflict this procedure is also followed or should be followed, each incident should be examined, each case of a person being wounded or killed should be examined and I'm addressing you as an expert in this field. As an expert, you would say that this is the procedure followed.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is basically my answer but I should add something. If the number of casualties is great, then particular attention has to be paid to these forms of investigation, that is to say, the autopsies and the examinations of the bodies in order to determine how the wound was inflicted and how the person was killed, in order to determine whether all the people in a certain incident or in a group of incidents were killed in -- or were wounded in the same way and the doctrine of forensic medicine in wartime conditions is such. The principles are such that one tries to establish all the relevant elements. For example, it's necessary to establish whether new weapons or new chemical means are used. It is absolutely necessary to perform an autopsy regardless of where the incidents take place. Sometimes there is a great number of people who are killed in a certain conflict and then it's not possible to perform an autopsy in the field or in an area that is far away from an urban centre but later on, autopsies can be performed, for example, when you exhume people and so on. This is the only way of obtaining certain parameters that are essential in order to perform an autopsy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. If I remember this well, in response to a question put to you by the Defence, you said that during the bombing of Belgrade, you continued to perform your duties as an expert who would examine the wounded and the dead. My question relates to Sarajevo in particular. I think that you are familiar with the conditions that prevailed in that city during the period from 1992 to 1994. Do you think, and are you in a position to answer this question, because perhaps you don't know about the situation on the ground, the medical personnel and the means that you had at your disposal, the hospitals, et cetera, given these factors, was it possible to perform an examination, to analyse each incident in order to obtain specific results which would establish with certainty, or almost with certainty, the direction of fire, the cause of death, et cetera. Given what you know, could you confirm anything of this kind?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can confirm, I can affirm that autopsies could have been carried out because there are always conditions in existence to carry out autopsies and they should have been carried out and my starting point is also how we -- what we did in Belgrade, how we did in Belgrade and how it was in Sarajevo and I know there is a colleague, Ilija Dobrica, who is mentioned in the report, I know him personally although we haven't seen each other for 12 years, I think, we were at a conference and I was the presidency of the forensic medicine of Yugoslavia so I know all the colleagues from the former Yugoslavia and according to my information, they operated regularly. They carried out autopsies. Now, I don't know whether they did complete autopsies or just examination, I don't know, because I was not in contact with him so that I can confirm this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE EL MAHDI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Professor Dunjic, I also have a few questions for you. Several times it appears in your report that you would have liked to have had x-rays available in order to form your opinion. Did you see any x-ray at all in relation to any of these cases you have studied?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to say that I have seen, and that was actually on Sunday, three days ago, when I arrived, I saw that for incident number -- incident -- I think that was in incident number 13. Then I saw or rather it was shown to me in the photographs in the pictures - just a moment - it's when I saw the photographs, that is the x-rays, that was the first time that I saw and for all the other cases, I did not see a single one. This is this thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You refer to case number 13 and you said you have seen these x-rays only a couple of days ago. Yes.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you seen the transcripts of what happened in this court in relation to case number 13 and when did you receive these transcripts? Could you see them before you -- before you drafted your report?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in September and -- that I was writing this report. That was in September last year, and the transcripts were forwarded to me roughly at that time, I can't remember the exact date, but this x-ray, that's why I have put that in the report, that there should be an x-ray not knowing that it existed because that was only that I got it on Sunday when I arrived, the 16th but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me put the next question to you. You had the transcripts, you could look at them before you drafted your report; is that a correct understanding of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, partly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm talking about incidents 13. Yes. Did you study them?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I read the information as much as I was able to understand from the transcript to assess the situation medically, what's important for me, what's necessary for me for this and that's why I've asked for the x-rays. They could not be found or rather they were not around at the time, I don't know why, because there was just the whole pile of photographs and now when we were sorting out the documents, then I saw that the photograph, in fact, that is, the x-ray in this case did exist which is why I brought it along and that's why I wanted to show this to you to say that this is one document and one -- there is also one document from a number 21 when there is a complete medical history while the first time when I was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When I am interested to know about incident 21, I'll ask you. So you were not surprised to see this x-ray a couple of days ago.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am surprised that I saw it but I can see that it's mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you ask for it previously?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I asked for complete documentation for all the cases, that is all the photos and x-rays, everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. And then when you studied the transcript while preparing your report, were you confronted with these x-rays, did you then address those who instructed you and would you ask them, you say "there must be x-rays, please provide them to me," or did you not specifically ask for it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't -- I didn't specifically ask for this x-ray. I generally asked for every incident, all the documentation, all the medical documents that existed including the x-rays, for instance, that I mentioned. Now, in my expert report, you have seen it, I founded it primarily on medical facts and these were just leading points for me, the statements, the testimonies, and the police report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were you aware, when you drafted your report, that x-ray did exist?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I knew that from the information that was mentioned by the witness in his statement or in his testimony, but I can only write a report on the basis of what I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but you did not write, unfortunately, "I have not seen the existing x-rays which disenabled me to draw further conclusions," but you do write "There are no detailed description of the mentioned wound in the medical documentation, neither x-ray snapshots." So you write that there are no x-ray snapshots.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am writing a report on the basis of what I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That answer is -- do you have -- have you seen one x-ray or more x-rays on incident 13?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unless I am mistaken, there are three photographs of an x-ray.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My next question would be: Could you please look, again - Madam Registrar, could you assist me - at some of these sketches you made? I'll select two for you. Could you please put them on the ELMO, if possible. Do you agree with me that the sketch you made where it reads case 4, that you used that when examined in chief about incident number four?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And you agree with me that the sketch on the left-hand side, you used that when asked about the consistency between the statement of Witness G with the direction of fire indicated by him? Would you agree with me that the angle under which the arrow approaches the body in the right picture is different from the angle on the left picture?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I've understood you correctly, Your Honour, are you saying about this angle, about the angle of the body and the arrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm talking about the angle between the arrow indicated and I would say the axis of the shoulders of the body you sketched.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, yes, yes, now I understood you. It's the angle of the shoulder and the arrow so this body should have been more like this, at this angle. That should have been parallel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the explanation you gave via drafting the black sketch was a bit different from the green sketch?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recall, what I did with the black pen, that was in relation to the question that I was asked by the Prosecutor in relation to the testimony of the witness and I can again make another drawing now and make it parallel so that we avoid any misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not asking you, I just wanted to --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Whether we agree on the fact that there is a different difference in the angle in which the right arrow approaches the body compared to the axis of the shoulders and the left sketch, the black one. Yes? If you'd like to explain anything further, I'll give you an opportunity to do so because you wanted to make a new sketch but would you just tell us first what you would like to explain to us.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I wanted to say, it's just because if -- now, if I sketched it now, it would be a different angle but what's important in order to understand what I'm trying to say is that in relation to the location of the wound, according to the witness testimony and the medical documentation, the direction that was shown by the witness where the fire had come from, in both cases, these directions do not correspond with the channel which I don't know -- for which I don't know what kind it is. I don't know the direction of that channel. That's why I've put three arrows. Here too, I could have put three arrows, but again it's this direction according to the medical documentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the question, when put to you in respect of the black drawing ignored the medical documentation, it was just about what the witness had told us. Yes. Then my next question would be: If you would exhumate a body after ten years, would you generally be able to still find reliably the wound channel if it only did hit soft tissue, if the projectile only did hit soft tissue?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say what the doctrine position is. The exhumation always gives a positive result. That means whether it confirms something, an assumption or whether it will refute it. In that sense that is a positive result. If there is no soft tissue then we will look for the bone tissue, I don't know what we will find but in these cases I noted one incident, for instance, number five when ricochet is mentioned about a hard surface. So I expect that if the exhumation is done, that the projectile will be found in the body because no one is talking about the exit wound and nobody noticed it and then there is an entry wound in the thigh area. What would we gain by an exhumation? If soft tissue was injured.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm not asking in general terms what we would gain by an exhumation because you explained that clearly in your report that we would gain something by an exhumation. I'm asking you whether, if a projectile would have hit only soft tissue, whether you would be able to identify the wound channel after ten years in soft tissue. I'm not asking whether you could find still the projectile or whether if it would have hit the bone, whether you could see something in the bone, I'm just asking you whether you would be able to identify, after ten years, a wound channel in soft tissue.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the case if there was a complete decomposition of soft tissue and only skeleton is left of course we couldn't possibly, but I don't know what we can find because it could happen that a body could be mummified, that is, that the skin would be completely saponified or it would be completely dried, so within that tissue it might be possible to find the channel if such changes have occurred but I am reiterating I don't know what we would encounter first it would have to do it and then we would have to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you say perhaps it's possible, perhaps it's not possible. Perhaps you will be able to identify such a wound channel and perhaps not. Could you tell us the decomposition of soft tissue under general conditions because I do understand that it depends on perhaps the humidity and all kind of other circumstances but in general, after how much time you would not find soft tissue that would allow you to identify a wound channel.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Soft tissue as a rule decomposes itself depending on the weather condition, external, internal conditions, on the place of burial, whether it had been already exhumed once and of course all the elements in the body itself, the form, the cause of death, inflammation, processes and so on. So I would say that in some average conditions of humidity, temperature of the soil, average conditions at the time of the burial, if the body was buried straight away and not certainly days later so that the decomposition, the putrification didn't start outside in the air then we can expect complete decomposition of the soft tissue and then after 7 to 15 years. That again depends on climatic conditions and that is very individual on an average. But I have already done autopsies after three months where there was a skeletalisation of the body without any soft tissue and I have done also autopsy after eight years where soft tissue was completely dried so there is no such a thing as a standard it's very dependent on different influences but that's what -- when there is wounding by firearm, when various types of projectiles are suspected then always it's an x-ray can be used the beginning of autopsy to see whether there are any fragments then we can see what kind of projectile was used and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My next question would be if a general practitioner or a emergency station doctor would see a patient with a shot wound, would he be able to give all the data you would need as a forensic medical expert? I mean is the knowledge and the skill of an ordinary doctor or someone who works in an emergency station, would that be sufficient to give you all the data you would need for an expert report? You told us what you actually needed; do you expect a normal doctor would be able to provide you with this information?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must tell you as a professor at the Faculty of Medicine, as far as our students are concerned in the entire region of the former Yugoslavia and I believe this is the same thing elsewhere in Europe, abroad, what we teach them is that they have to stick to some standards that are needed for forensic purposes which means that they have to do a precise location of the wound to be able to describe it. These are two important standards. I know that in emergency medicine, that is in the emergency treatment, injuries have to be attended to or emergency surgery. But following that, after the treatment has been administered, every doctor has to write a medical report about what he has done and that's when he has to use the methodology that will be useful for forensic purposes. That means he does not have to describe everything that we would do as forensic experts, but what is necessary to describe that this defect in the skin is regular, he can just say roughly one centimetre but he has to locate the wound precisely and he has to write it as a diagnosis in Latin so what I have told you vulnus transsclopetarium, reg. Femuris, et cetera in on case. That would be shotgun wound of the right thigh, and that's when we need the extra bit, two wounds, one to the front, one to the back. He doesn't even have to specify whether the entry is front and exit is back or the other way around but he must describe it that there are two wounds that there is a wound here and that there is a wound there and possibly the diameter of the wounds but this is what's missing here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I know what's missing. You have described that in great detail, Professor Dunjic. You say it would have to describe that, let me try to make it quite simple, would a normal general practitioner or a emergency station doctor, would he be able, for example, to make a clear distinction between an oval entry wound you explained to us that you would find that if the shot was fired at a certain angle or a more circular, is this a kind of distinction a normal doctor -- would you expect a normal doctor to make such a distinction?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of the doctors, even if they see it, they will not describe it. That's what I know from practice. Your Honour, he doesn't have to describe the wound, whether it is an oval or whether it is a circle, that's not so important, but it's very important whether there are two wounds or three wounds and to see whether there is a link between them, that's very important. If he describes two wounds then it is very easy for us to establish with an examination whether they've been linked, what's entry, what's exit, but you must say that they exist, he must at least describe what their size is and to give Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. precise location again this is individual because our students generally speaking medical students when they come to the fifth or sixth year of medical studies all of these photographs that I was -- all these sketches, all these photographs that I was making but in the original, we teach them how to recognise the wound, what type of wounds there are, how is a wound by a projectile, how is a wound by a knife, all these -- what's a stab and so on and this is what they have to study for an exam and they have to take the exam within the subject that I teach.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, is it an obligatory for all those who are studying medicine who want to become a doctor to follow the courses in forensic medicine? Is it optional or is it obligatory?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obligatory subject in our faculty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I have one final question for you: When studying the case number four of which we spoke about a lot, did you also -- first of all, let me ask you whether you saw the transcript and what transcript, because he asked you about transcripts yesterday. Could you still tell us what transcript you did see?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I looked at the CD with all the transcripts and here I have the documents that I've already showed you and I know what transcript is, with all the numbers just like it's here on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you know the date of the transcript you studied?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. And in the first statement that I read, and that I used --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, do you remember what dates of transcript you --

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, really. I don't. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic, in your list, it says the 28th of January, 2002; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I think that is the date of the transcript when Mr. L was heard, no, sorry, Mr. G, that's incident number four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He was examined on two days, not only on the 28th but I -- so the expert witness has not seen the transcript of the 25th of January; is that correct, since you indicate that it was the 28th.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as far as I know, the professor looked at the disc on which all the transcripts were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So your list is not of great use because he has -- might have consulted all the transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... In the letter is first of all the Professor has been made available Professor Dunjic all the transcripts of all the witnesses or ...

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The only problem was the time and I was trying to be precise in relation to the letter of my learned colleague and the professor arrived on Sunday and that's -- so we wanted to send the letter to Mr. Ierace on that day so it wasn't just a transcript, all the other documents. That's obvious from the letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then do you remember what actually the Witness G described that he was doing when he was hit, and did you take that into consideration?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recall from his testimony, he had heard some shots and so he lay on the ground and after a couple of minutes, he got up just to -- I think it was to pick lettuce or something and then that position, he was half crouching, that's when, as he was shown on the recording, he was hit in the back and the projectile hit him somewhere in the area of the right shoulder in the back and that's what the Prosecutor asked me about yesterday, but that's what I'm saying to you today. This what he said, the testimony, does not correspond to the medical documentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Either one of them should be true, is that a correct understanding of your testimony that if something does not --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One is right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One of them is right and the other one would not be right.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Someone is right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Do you have any, if you say, picking -- no, I have no further questions for you. Is there any need to put any further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, we'll have a few questions after your last questions but I'm taking note of the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. How much time would you need for your questions, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That depends to a large extent on the answers, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You know that it's also, to some extent, in your own hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, not much time, five or ten minutes at the most, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps if we could conclude now, but that would then be within five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gladly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Then I would finish in five minutes. Yes, then I take it that you would like to have these sketches again on the ELMO. Mr. Usher, could you please put them again on the ELMO. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, witness. Could you take the pointer, please. Could you point it at the green figure. Don't move it anymore. Put it where you put it a minute ago, please. There we are, stop. What is the object drawn above your pointer? It's an elongated form at the bottom of the green drawing?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This part here?

utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to depict the right arm which was stretched out.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, would you agree with me that in the parallel figure, the black figure that is next to the green one, could you put your pointer on the black figure, the other drawing. Thank you. Would you agree with me that this anatomical detail doesn't appear in this figure?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, to the best of your recollection, to the extent that you can remember the hearing of yesterday, wouldn't it be true to say that this second drawing -- I'll withdraw that. Could you say what the full black arrows represent that we can see in the black drawing? The full black arrows, below, below.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These arrows here?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes exactly what are they?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They represent the possible channel wounds according to the witness statements and these are the possible points of entry of the projectile for those channels.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Would it be correct to say that this drawing depicts four possible -- four possibilities that relate to the entry and the exit?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are four possible directions here, there could be many more. I've only indicated three here, but what I've drawn here, this is the direction indicated by the witness. This isn't to be taken into consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, could you please your answer my question. Thank you very much. I'm going to move on to another subject. Mr. President -- and I would like you to just answer this question, Mr. President asked you about young practitioners who are not as experienced as you in your field, young interns and they weren't that experienced in their missions in hospitals or in treatment centres, in clinics, my question is as follows, if one does not have the professional experience that you have and one sees several wounds inflicted by bullets in wartime circumstances, if a doctor sees such wounds does one gain or not gain practical experience which would help him determine immediately the point of entry and the point of exit and I'm talking about the experience obtained by the medical corps. Could you briefly respond to that? It's not a forensic expert.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They have some general experience about what an entry and exit wound looks like but that doesn't mean anything. They have to take care, they have to treat the wound, but it is also their duty to describe these wounds precisely. They have to describe the size of the wound as I explained to Mr. President, they have to do this obviously this isn't done immediately this is done at a later date.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think with your permission, Ms. Pilipovic has one more question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You should do it quickly and we're running out of tape and I said five more minutes so please, Ms. Pilipovic, one more question.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Professor, yesterday you spoke about a document. My question arises from one of the questions put to you by Judge El Mahdi with regard to autopsies. The certificate that you interpreted with regard to incident number 12, can you say -- incident number 11, can you say whether an autopsy was performed and when can such a certificate be issued?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such a certificate is issued when an external examination of the body is carried out or when an autopsy is performed but from this document we cannot obtain whether an autopsy was performed.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise this incident took place on the 7th of September, 1993 and the examination was the autopsy according to the certificate that you examined was performed on the 9th of September 1993?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN DUNJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, two days afterwards, that's customary.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This concludes your testimony in this Court, Professor Dunjic. One question for you is whether you would be willing to leave your sketches behind so that if one of the parties would like to have that in evidence then we could use it or -- it's your property, if you want to take it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, they are available for us. Then I'd like to thank you very much for coming today. Mr. Usher, would you please collect the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and making your expertise available to this Chamber and answering questions of both parties and of the Chamber. Thank you very much for coming and I wish you to safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to thank you too, and I would just like to add if it's necessary to perform an examination or carry out exhumations I'm at your disposal, I am at the disposal of the Defence, Prosecution, I'm at everyone's disposal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Usher could you please escort Professor Dunjic out of the courtroom. At the suggestion of Madam Registrar, I suggest that we'll deal with the documents tomorrow. It's a bit of -- there are some confusing but we'll sort them out. If the parties would like to have a look at them again, they are available with the registry in order to make up your mind whether you want to tender them into evidence or have them marked for identification. utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much. Mr. Gray, please be seated. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, is it you, you will just be examined by counsel for the Defence.
