utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I wish to make a submission in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then Mr. Usher could you please -- we'll have to -- there is a procedural issue the parties would like to address the Chamber and that is usually done, if it relates to your testimony, in your absence so may I ask you just to follow the usher for one second and to leave the courtroom so that the parties could address the court as they wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll turn it to private session or -- yes, we'll turn it to private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, could you please tell us when you arrived in Sarajevo, which year, which month?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: I arrived in Sarajevo on the 10th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. And how long did you stay there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: I departed Sarajevo on the 20th of September, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. During that entire period, did you ever leave Sarajevo; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. For how long, for what period of time and on how many occasions?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: I departed on two occasions and I would like to refer to my diary to --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Please go ahead. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Okay. I will refer to my diary to actually get those actual details. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Ask the witness to find that during the next break and, Mr. Gray, would you first now concentrate again on other questions and may I invite you to look for the date of departure from Sarajevo during the next break.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I can see that you are wearing a number of medals for the first time. I would appreciate if you could tell us why you are wearing those medals very briefly?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: That is the Order of the British Empire, operational service medal.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think it's very relevant given the matters that were raised a minute ago. I think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the Chamber allows you to -- please continue. You started with the Order of the British Empire.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Order of the British Empire, Operational Service Medal, Lebanon, UNPROFOR, Long Service, Rhodesia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, how is one awarded such medals?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: By hard graft, by being there and doing what you're required to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. With regard to this matter, return to the subject of Sarajevo, did you personally know General Galic while you were in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you meet him on more than one occasion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Could you tell us approximately how many times you met him, for example, more than five or more than ten times, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: I met him on approximately every other day, I mean -- I mean I met him on every other day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So we could say that you met him very frequently?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you saw him so frequently, what could you tell us about his personality and I'm not referring to his military capacity, I'm talking about the person himself?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: He was a very personable, I mean a very pleasant person to meet and talk with.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. You have said that he was a very pleasant person, what do you mean by pleasant?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: I mean that he was a nice person. I mean someone that you could be friendly with. I mean a nice person, I mean someone -- someone who you would have no fears about sharing your problems with or anything else like that. He was a nice person -- is a nice person.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Witness, I would now like to discuss matters that concern humanity, I'm not talking about humanitarian matters. Did you ever hear General Galic say anything that might have been unnecessarily wounding to the other side? Did he ever say anything on a racist nature with regard to the other side, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Are you certain about that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, on the basis of your experience in Sarajevo while you were there, can you tell us where you stayed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Okay. I initially stayed in a hotel, then I moved from the hotel and I -- I arranged for five apartments for the military observers who were staying there. I did that, then we stayed in those apartments and then on the --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Stop you there, I apologise but we have to establish fairly precise chronological order. What was the name of the hotel, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: It was I think the Mojmilo or something like that hotel. It was Mojmilo hotel and then we moved into apartments and then on the -- when the war started in Sarajevo which happened on the 14th of May, yeah, 14th of May, that's the one. That's when the war started really in Sarajevo and then on the 15th and 16th of May, we had to move out and we actually moved into the PTT building and that's where we stayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, would you be able to recognise the places that you have just mentioned on a map? Could you recognise the PTT building on a map, for example? Witness, with the assistance of the usher and if the Chamber allows us to do so, we are going to show you two parts of a map. It's going to be handed down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Mr. Gray, would you please wait until a map has been presented to you and in order to avoid whatever confusion not use any other map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, if you have to write something, if you would want to write something, you have to do so by using a black pen for practical reasons. The usher will provide you with one immediately. I hope it will be -- I hope the tip will be fine enough?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I ask you only to mark anything on the map, Mr. Gray, if you are invited to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Mr. Gray, could you take what we call the pointer, first of all, and could you point to the PTT building on the map? I don't know if the technical booth could zoom in, perhaps, and focus on that now.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. The witness pointed to the building to the south of Miljacka, the so-called PTT building. Witness, could you tell us where the first hotel in which you resided was located and then could you point to the buildings that you have mentioned, if you find these places on the map?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Yeah, okay. Sure, okay. This is the Rainbow hotel here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I'll stop you there, you mentioned the Mojmilo hotel would that be the same one?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Or is it the Rainbow?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: The Rainbow hotel is further to the west--

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just stop you, Mr. Gray.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Perhaps the ELMO could be zoomed back and the witness be invited to indicate that position again so that we can follow it on the screen. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please point again to where the hotel was, Mr. Gray.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Rainbow hotel?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Yes, please start with the Rainbow.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: The Rainbow hotel is here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: The witness pointed to the south of the main road close to a spaghetti junction to the west next to the Oslobodjenje building. Could you point to the flats that you had to find for your military observers?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. The witness pointed to the area known as Alipasino Polje. Thank you. Could you now take a black pen and mark with the number one, could you mark the PTT building with number one?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you do the same thing for the Rainbow Hotel, mark it with number two?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. And could you do the same thing for the approximate location of the flats?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, just for your guidance if you invite the witness to mark on the map, it's not necessary to first tell us very precisely what he points at because that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I know why I'm doing this, Mr. President. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, since we've been referring to these flats, could you briefly tell us what your duties were in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: I was first in Sarajevo and I was brought to Sarajevo -- originally I was in Knin which is obviously away from Sarajevo. I was brought to Sarajevo because of my experience -- whatever. And I was brought there as the chief operations officer for the military observer group in the whole of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: What was your rank at the time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: What was your rank when you left Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. So you were promoted in the interim period?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, you mentioned the PTT building. I have a number of questions and we're going to focus on this geographical area of the town. As far as you know, can you tell us whether the PTT building had a basement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: It had two sub-basements, two, not one, but two.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you describe both of these basements; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Would you do so, please?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Okay. One sub-basement was a parking area and the second sub-basement was an engineering workshop, it was -- I mean a full engineering workshop. It was there, it had lathes, I mean I did metal work at school -- okay. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I'll stop you there. I'm sorry. These two areas, we'll go back to the workshop, were these two areas divided by a wall, by a barrier? What separated these two areas?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Okay. I mean they were separated by, I mean, concrete floors so I mean one was here and one was there. They were separated in terms of the rest of the building by doors.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Could you describe the doors, were they made of wood, of metal?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Well, on the 14th, 15th, 16th 17th of May, the doors were broken and the doors were repaired later. I was very, very busy doing negotiating with the parties but the doors were smashed in. They were repaired and they had at the very top of the door a panel -- a glass panel which had been broken, but this -- this plus the doors was totally screened over, I mean it was -- metal was actually put over it so that no one could see in.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that no one could see through, that nevertheless, who was present in the interior, in the second part of the basement, as far as you know? You spoke about a workshop, what do you know about this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: The workshop which is shown on -- I mean -- it is on video so I mean it's there. The workshop was used to produce weapons and repair weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I have something to say in the absence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll do it differently. Mr. Gray, we are about to have a break. We usually have two breaks in the afternoon. I'm aware that you might not like it to go in and out of the courtroom, I hope that then for the next hour we'll continue but we'll adjourn until five minutes past 6.00 so we have a break. That's also for the interpreters because they have to interpret whatever has to be said and they can't just go on for hours and hours so that's one of the reasons why we at a certain frequency have a break. Mr. Usher, could you first escort Mr. Gray out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, do we have to turn into private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll then turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are in open session again. The Chamber is aware of the problems the Defence faces and as a consequence, the Prosecution also faces and we'll ensure that the Prosecution will have extra time if they -- if there is extra time is needed for a proper preparation of the cross-examination of the witness and although we are in the late stage of the proceedings, the Chamber will ensure that no unfairness, other than inevitable, sometimes things are not for the full 100 per cent fair because of reasons that are beyond the control of the parties and the Chamber. That's part of life, I would say, but we'll -- we are fully aware of the problems. Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. In the meantime, Mr. President, we availed ourself of the opportunity to link up with the Prosecution but we'll see about it later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, let us go back to the question of the PTT building and of the second of those workshops that you spoke about before the break, those locations. You mentioned that there was a workshop, what do you know about it and what can you tell us about it, please?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Okay. The workshop itself was very extensive. It would have been at least 100 metres long by 50 metres wide, I mean it covered the whole basement of the PTT. It had heavy machinery in there, lathes, a lot of welding machinery there. It was designed as a workshop to manufacture material for the PTT.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us now, at the time of your stay in Sarajevo, how was this workshop used, for what purpose?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: When the -- when we first arrived in Sarajevo, the -- we took over the PTT building as the UN headquarters and so the workshop was not used for anything at all. However, after the events of the 14th of May, and then the 8th of June, and the withdrawal basically of the UN forces from Sarajevo, and all -- all that was left behind were ten military observers and 30 French soldiers, I mean that's all that was left after. There were a couple of Swedish cooks but I mean that's all that was left. We used the workshop area initially for a generator to actually supply power to actually recharge the handy talkies that we had so we could actually talk to each other and the bay stations so we could talk to each other, for lighting, but that only lasted for about a week and then we stopped and we moved the generator up into the car park and the workshop area was then vacated and it then was taken over by the Bosnian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. This workshop was taken over by the so-called Presidency forces, but to what purpose, as far as you know, what did they do there, practically speaking?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I have a videotape which I provided for the Defence. They repaired weapons there, they manufactured weapons there, they sealed the doors so that no one could see in or -- I mean, see what they were doing. They took in and removed, by night, weapons which they then used to fire at the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, you're telling us that the doors were sealed in such a way that one could not see inside, but how were you able to find out about this, about what was happening in that workshop?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Well, I have -- I have the videotape and also I know that I saw vehicles coming and leaving at night to the workshop.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And what did they offload or unload, if they were doing that? What were these vehicles doing?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: They were delivering materiel to be repaired, I mean, damaged weapons and they were taking away repaired weapons and they were also manufacturing other weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Colonel, did you see this with your own eyes?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: I saw the vehicles coming and going, but I didn't actually see -- I mean -- I mean I wasn't invited in to actually see them remanufacturing weapon -- I mean, no one -- I mean they kept us out of there. I mean, the doors were padlocked, they were screened. You couldn't see in and quite frankly, I had other things to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. But my question is precisely as follows: Did you see vehicles bringing arms, weapons, even ammunitions, bringing them there?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: I saw vehicles that arrived. You have to understand that it was an underground workshop so I mean it was -- it was underground. I mean and I took refugees from the same place at a different level, but I mean -- you have to understand that you couldn't see in. All I saw was I mean vehicles arriving and departing. That's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, you speak to us about -- no, I withdraw that. You speak to us about weapons. Can you tell us, if you were able to see in the surrounding area of the PTT building anything else in relation to weapons of one side or the other side?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Yes, I can. We had one incident where there were two tanks from the Bosnian forces which were parked 50 metres away from the PTT building. I went down by myself and I spoke to them and said, "You have to move away," and they said, well, their commander was away at the Rainbow hotel having lunch. The Rainbow hotel was approximately 400 metres away from the PTT and they couldn't give me any answer until he came back. So I went back and I got an interpreter and we went back again and I said well, "unless you move your tanks, I'll have a Ukrainian company come and they will move you one way or the other." And very shortly thereafter, they did move the tanks away but they parked them by the PTT for the reason that the PTT and the UN headquarters gave them protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us anything else, Colonel, in relation to other types of weapons that you are able to observe around the PTT building, to start with?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Not around the PTT.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Are there any other locations in Sarajevo where you, yourself, physically saw weapons that belonged, of course, to the so-called Presidency forces?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: There were many locations that I saw weapons that belonged to the Presidency forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Could you, Witness, indicate these locations on the map which is to your right? Sorry, to your left, my mistake. If you could please leave the map on the ELMO in such a way that we can see it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Here --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Given the period of time that this witness was in Sarajevo, both before the indictment period and during the indictment period, I would respectfully seek that in relation to this these positions, it is made clear whether the periods relate to pre-indictment or post-indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's coming.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do take it you ask the witness what he say and he told us when he left Sarajevo, was it the 10th of September.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: 20th September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You arrived on the 10th.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 5th of April and I left on the 20th of September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, could you please indicate, again, with the pointer, the areas where you saw the weapons.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I would be grateful if you can take a black felt-tip pen, please, and if you can place number 4 on the location that you've just indicated.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps the witness could be given a pen that actually works.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a moment, just a moment, witness. Okay. Thank you. Could you tell us what did you see with your own eyes on the places that are indicated first under number 4 and then under number 5?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Okay. Number 4, there were two tanks, okay, T55s and they were parked in a tunnel, okay, one out of view or anything else. Okay, and number 5, there was one tank and four APCs or armoured personnel carriers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. I'm just going to interrupt you, Witness. The number 5 is located in a green area on the map which indicates, as we can see the symbols, it's indicating a cemetery. Are you absolutely certain of the position of these weapons in the cemetery in question?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Absolutely positive.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. How come that you can be so certain of that, why is that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Because I saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. What were they looking for in terms of protection in that area?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: They were parked underneath trees, okay, for camouflage.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what was the time period when you saw these weapons, I'm not talking about a specific date, but a month, was it the beginning of your stay or the end, whatever?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: It was at the time that we actually deployed our military observers for the Papa side, the Presidency side, that was Papa, Lima was the Serb side which was Lima was for Lukavica. That's what Papa and Lima stood for. And we saw them at the time we actually deployed the military observers to try and observe the weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Do you remember, witness, of the month, more or less, that you saw that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: I can give you the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well, even better, thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. No problem. Okay. Here we go. That was Lima side. It would have been about the -- it would have been about the 3rd of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you have an opportunity to see these weapons later during your stay in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: I saw them when we deployed the military observers. We deployed them to --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Don't write anything, please don't write anything for the moment.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Can you just answer the question that I've asked? Did you have an opportunity to see them -- to see these weapons later?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: I saw them on at least two other occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you locate, more or less in time, can you tell us a month, was it in August, in September or still in July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: No, it was still in July.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, did you see other weapons in Sarajevo and, if so, which ones?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I saw 105 Howitzers, I saw 120-millimetre mortars, 82-millimetre mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You're going too fast for me, witness. Where were the weapons that you have mentioned located? Let's start with the Howitzers.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Okay. The Howitzers were located up -- okay, let's get the right map. I believe there, they were located there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Could you please point to the area, you're talking about the Hum area; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please take a black felt-tip pen and mark it with number six.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: There's a very distinctive tower right next to where these guns were.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned other weapons, could you repeat which weapons you mentioned and tell us where they were located?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Okay. There were 120-millimetre mortars, 120-millimetre mortars, okay, they were located at the stadium here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Mark that area with number seven, please.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, and then ...

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: There were other weapons, I don't have the precise location but they are basically located here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Could you mark that with number eight, please?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And tell us which weapon is concerned?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: They were 120-millimetre mortars and 82-millimetre mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Any other locations in the city, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: There were many other locations, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Could you indicate some other locations that you can remember?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Do you want these in the city or do you want --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I'm only talking about the interior of the part which was under the control of the so-called Presidency forces, that is to say, I'm talking about the Papa side?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Okay. No, I can't with any accuracy, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, could you please tell us if you were -- I apologise, I'll withdraw that. Did you see any other mechanical means, any other mechanical devices apart from tanks and APCs and fixed mortars?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: My people, my observers observed vehicles, light trucks, which had the top removed, they had them cut out and these were being used as mobile mortar bases in order that they could fire and then leave and avoid the retaliatory fire which would come from the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Colonel, you have mentioned retaliatory fire, is that also what we call "counter-battery fire," that's a technical term that we sometimes use?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: That's true. That's absolutely true.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, why did the Presidency forces open fire like this, in your opinion, if you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: They opened fire in many cases with full knowledge that they would receive counter-battery fire, but they did this with the full knowledge that they would have full media attention when they did this.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object. The question invites this type of speculation it's more appropriate for the witness to be asked what he knows and that to be distinguished from what opinions he might have. But the first thing what does he know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Will you please ask for facts, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, rather than --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, who is Mr. Carrington?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Lord Carrington was the foreign secretary for the U.K.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Who is Mr. Carrington, or rather Lord Carrington, if we're talking about Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: He was one of the many individual politicians who came to try and bring some peace to --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. The same question for Lord Owen?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, did you have any experience in Sarajevo with regard to the arrival of one of these men in Sarajevo and if so, what could you tell us about this experience, please?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Okay, this is a goody. Okay. We had a visit of Lord Carrington on the 3rd of July, 1992. It wasn't a good day. I've got it on videotape. We --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, we can talk about the date later, but can you just remind us of the events, Lord Carrington arrived in Sarajevo, where were you, what were you doing?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Okay. As the senior military observer, I was required to be in presence when they met at the Presidency and you have to understand that the meeting schedule was kept quite separate and so one side wasn't aware of the timing of when the other side was meeting with the politician who was in Sarajevo at the time to actually try and resolve the whole problem. So what happened was that he had already gone and he'd met at the airport the Serbian side and they'd been brought from Lukavica to actually have that meeting. There was then a delay and so he was 30 minutes late in actually getting to the Presidency to meet the Bosnian Muslim, whatever, Presidency side. They had very carefully placed out a cordon of police which stretched down the opposite side from the Presidency and the police were set at 10-metre intervals, et cetera. We were told that he was late and that was fine, I mean it was UN time, and then we were told he was coming. The police moved as I was looking from the front of the Presidency, they were -- they moved from left to right. Immediately after that, and while he was actually on his way, two mortar bombs landed, 82-millimetre mortar bombs and I know the difference between 82, 120, 122, 105, I've been through it, they landed and they killed people and wounded people right there. An ambulance arrived no longer than 30 seconds after the bombs had landed. The police moved back. I was standing in the entrance with liaison officers from the Bosnian Presidency. They actually moved inside the building and left me standing outside the front, which I thought was really nice, when the bombs actually landed because they knew they were coming. It was quite deliberate, very premeditated and the thing is that the Serbs had no idea, they had no visual contact with the actual impact area, they didn't know what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I apologise, I'll stop you there. You said the Serbs didn't know, what can you tell us, for example, did you hear the shots being fired, the shells being fired from mortars and if you did, what can you tell us about this on the basis of what you have heard?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: I've done, in my 30 years in the army, I've done a number of courses, one of them was on heavy weapons, including mortars. I know exactly, I mean, I fired them so I know precisely what a mortar sounds like when it is fired, okay? It has a very distinctive sound, okay. As I was standing outside the front door of the Presidency, I heard the primary go off. The mortars were fired from less than 200 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I'll stop you there, witness. We're not experts and this is why I'm interrupting you. Could you briefly tell us what a primary is?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Okay. A mortar bomb has a primary which is in the very base of the tailfin and then it has a number of charges which are put round the side of it to actually add distance to it but if you fire a mortar just on primary without any charges around it, then it will go a maximum of 200 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. So what did you conclude on the basis of the position that was hit by the shells? What could you conclude with regard to the origin of fire?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: It had to come from the Presidency side, the Muslim side. It was totally deliberate. It was premeditated murder.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I asked you this series of questions because a minute ago you spoke about media coverage. What could you tell us with regard to this specific incident and as far as such media coverage is concerned?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Well, the media are obviously there already anyway to get all the clips of Lord Carrington and whatever arriving so I mean they were there anyway, but, I mean, it was all arranged for Carrington and the media. Carrington drove through the slaughter, okay, and the ambulances and everything else and all the sirens and whatever. I mean he drove through all of that to come to the meeting. And by the way, while we actually had the meeting which I attended myself, we had a few mortar bombs land just for good effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, thank you. I'll come back to the issue of the -- of media coverage but my question now is as follows: Were you personally affected, as a man, by this experience?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Of course I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's turn to the issue of media coverage. You spoke about shells being fired from mobile mortars and you told this Chamber that this was done in order to obtain media coverage, you provided us with a very specific example. Can you tell us what you heard in regard to fire being opened from these mobile mortars. What did you hear in relation to media coverage?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [In English] What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY
utterances.text: What we had from the Papa side was reports from military observers about these trucks, vans, light trucks, that were being used to fire mortars indiscriminately at the Serb side and then obviously fire was coming back from the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have other questions but we're running out of time. It's time to adjourn. Is it time to adjourn before Mr. Ierace arises.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we adjourn for the day, Mr. Ierace, is there anything that you would like to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: To save time for tomorrow, I notice the witness has referred to a diary. We haven't been given a copy of that, wonder if it could be produced. Perhaps to the registrar so we can have photocopy it. I notice the witness referring to a map I don't know if it's a plain map or a marked map but perhaps we could have a copy of that to save time for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we gladly use our time to copy all the pages of these diary and to provide the Prosecution with them in the course of the night. I have only just found out about the existence of this diary but we need time to do this we shouldn't -- if we're to copy all the documents, I don't know how many pages there are, I can't do it now, perhaps tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Will it be possible, Madam Registrar, to even, if necessary, we might find someone, perhaps not four persons, but we might find someone who will -- could do it. We should be willing to give you a diary, I hope your handwriting is such that we could read it so that we could see what is in it and so that the parties could -- would you be willing to give it to the Chamber? Yes. Thank you. Then as far as the map is concerned, are there any markings on this map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There will be any questions about the map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I also have a trace which goes on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, given the time, I don't think that there will be any questions about that map because in order to save time, we're going to use one map alone but we could copy it too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But it's at least available to the parties would you be willing to give us a copy of these maps.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will get the originals returned.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, the registrar will assist with this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you very much, Madam Registrar. Then is there anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. In order to be able to work on this, I'd like to inform the registrar that we can be reached at all times and if this work is completed even late at night, you shouldn't hesitate to call us. We are at your disposal. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... The Prosecution could be reached, Mr. Ierace; is that correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Sorry I didn't hear that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that a telephone number is available to the registry where the Prosecution could be reached this evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. President, in relation to the videotapes, I think my friend wants them back tonight. I'm happy to do that but again it means that we won't have a chance to look at them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we need time. Is there no way of copying them? I mean copying videotapes should not take necessarily the full time. I think it's even called dubbing if you to do it at a quick speed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I asked the technicians whether there was a possibility of doing this and they told me that such a machine still has to be invented so if we have four times two and a half hours or two hours, that's eight hours of copying that we are faced with and this is a problem and I can't resolve it personally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Mr. Piletta-Zanin has the Defence been --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, in order to save time, I allowed myself to question this witness about the contents of these videos and the witness told me about certain events that should be of interest to justice. We have filtered out some of these elements and I actually saw one of the cassettes but not the others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Sit together and look at a videotape together but it would save a lot of time, perhaps divided by a little screen and looking at the same screen in front of you but so you see some creativity in solving the problems. Let's be aware, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, that if you are provided at a late stage with the video material that it does not only cause a problem for you but for the Prosecution as well so we'll have to grant sufficient time so therefore, I'm just wondering whether one could connect two video monitors to one video recorder so you don't have to copy it but even in separate rooms you could look at the same thing and perhaps first a going through so that at least you know what is approximately there as images. Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, when I look at the video like that, sometimes I want to stop and go back and check and so on. Another solution which I suggested to my learned colleague is that if we can -- if he can look at it in the building complex in the Defence room if they've got a video machine available. While he's looking at one I can look at another and we can swap them over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you can exchange if you don't look at them in chronological order. May I really urge the parties to see how we can prevent that -- the tomorrow or the day after tomorrow the Prosecution could look at the videos. For adults it may be able to reach a solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, one of the solutions comes to mind quite naturally is as follows: We have identified in the first cassette things that to us appear as the most interesting ones for the purposes of justice and what I suggest is to guide Mr. Ierace and tell him that this is the cassette that we are really going to rely on and I suggest that you view these parts. I will be faithful, trustworthy to the very end and I won't provide a different version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Legal practice for too long time to ignore that sometimes the assistance and the help of one party to the other could be interpreted by the other party in a different way so let's try to -- if you try to look at these videos in such a way that you look both at the same time, whether you guide each other or not but we do not lose any time. If there's any remaining problem, I will be available to the building to reconcile conflicting positions for at least some time this evening so a practical solution should be reached within the next hour I would say and I'm certainly still there. So if there's any need for my help, then please ask me. Mr. Gray.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have to stop for the evening.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know, but can I say something about the videotapes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In order to interpret what you actually are seeing, I need to be there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Certainly if the videos will be played in court and to the extent that they are not played, the Chamber is not aware of its content but certainly you will be asked questions about it but the parties should have the opportunity to see the whole of it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Even if there are things totally irrelevant on it, but first the parties should look at it and certainly will put questions to you in relation to the videos if they decide that they are relevant enough to be played in this court. We'll then adjourn. May I instruct you and could we please go into private session for one second?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll adjourn then until tomorrow at quarter past 2.00 Madam Registrar, I think in this same courtroom. I instruct you, Mr. Gray, not to speak with anyone about your testimony you've given until now or the testimony still to be given perhaps in the next day or two. We'll adjourn until tomorrow in the afternoon, quarter past 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: at 7.10 p.m., to be reconvened on Wednesday the 19th day of February, 2003, at 2.15 p.m.
